seo.metaDescription: Diabetic eye screening every 2 years: the study behind it, a North East London replay putting 39% of diagnoses a screen later, and what optometrists do.
seo.metaTitle: Diabetic eye screening every 2 years: what the data shows

keyPoints: Since October 2023, England has been moving people whose last 2 routine screens found no retinopathy to screening every 2 years, in stages. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland changed first.
The evidence was retrospective: of 354,549 people in 7 UK programmes, 0.3% to 1.3% of those with 2 clear screens progressed to referable retinopathy within 2 years.
Replaying North East London's records on a 2-year cycle put 39% of sight-threatening diagnoses a screen later, with more building up in groups already at higher risk.
The College asks optometrists to check when the last screen was, keep usual sight-test recall with judgement for higher-risk groups, and report what they find.

faq.a: Across the UK, people with diabetes aged 12 and over are offered screening, and all four nations now screen people at low risk every 2 years under their own programme rules. In England, low risk means no retinopathy in either eye at the last 2 routine screens. There, background retinopathy without maculopathy means yearly screening, maculopathy means OCT surveillance, and more advanced changes mean closer monitoring or a hospital referral. Pregnant women are screened more often.
faq.q: How often should you have diabetic eye screening?

faq.a: For the group it covers, the average risk is low. In the Four Nations study of 354,549 people, 0.3% to 1.3% of those with 2 clear screens progressed to referable retinopathy within 2 years. Liverpool's ISDR trial tested a risk calculator using clinical data, not England's rule, in a mostly white population: attendance was equivalent, and detection non-inferior within its 1.5-point margin (1.4% against 1.7%). A simulation on North East London's records found 39% of sight-threatening diagnoses after 2 clear screens would have come a screen later.
faq.q: Is diabetic eye screening every 2 years safe?

faq.a: The College of Optometrists says that for a patient in an NHS diabetic eye screening programme, sight-test recall should be the same as for someone without diabetes, whether screening is every 6, 12 or 24 months. It asks optometrists to use their judgement for younger people and people of Black and Asian ethnicities, who are affected by sight-threatening retinopathy more. An examination or photographs at a practice are not an alternative to the NHS screening programme, and the College asks optometrists to say so.
faq.q: How often should people with diabetes have an eye test?

faq.a: The UK National Screening Committee recommended it in 2016 for people at low risk of sight loss, after a large study found that few people with 2 clear screens progressed to referable retinopathy within 2 years. NHS England says the change frees appointments for people at higher risk and spares low-risk people a yearly visit. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland made the change before England, which followed from October 2023.
faq.q: Why did diabetic eye screening change to every 2 years?

body.text: In North East London's records, a 2-year gap between diabetic eye screens would have pushed 39% of sight-threatening diagnoses in people with 2 clear screens back a screen, a simulation [published in Diabetologia](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00125-025-06379-6) found. Since October 2023, England has been moving people whose last 2 routine screens found no retinopathy onto diabetic eye screening every 2 years instead of every year.

It follows a 2016 recommendation from the UK National Screening Committee, and Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland made the change before England. NHS England tells people on the longer interval to see their optometrist straight away if their sight changes.
Who is on diabetic eye screening every 2 years

In England it takes no retinopathy and no maculopathy in either eye (R0M0) at the last 2 routine screens. One microaneurysm makes a screen R1, and R1 alone means yearly screening again, while maculopathy (M1) means OCT surveillance. Pregnant women are screened more often. A review in Eye Open adds that people with type 1 diabetes starting a hybrid closed loop system are exempt, those starting an insulin pump stay yearly for a year, and the change has been staggered since a 2024 software upgrade.
What the evidence behind the change showed

The UK National Screening Committee relied on the Four Nations study, [published in Diabetes Care](https://doi.org/10.2337/dc14-1778). It pooled 2005 to 2012 grading results for 354,549 people in 7 programmes: the national ones of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and 4 in England. Of people with no retinopathy at 2 screens at least 12 months apart, 0.3% to 1.3% progressed to referable retinopathy within 2 years, and fewer than 0.3% to proliferative disease. With background retinopathy in both eyes at both screens, the figures were 13% to 29% and up to 4%.

It was retrospective, and its authors wrote that it could not directly show the effect of changing the interval. The nearest test is Liverpool's ISDR trial, which randomised 4,534 people to yearly screening or to 6, 12 or 24 months set by a risk calculator using clinical data. Attendance at first follow-up was equivalent (83.6% against 84.7%), sight-threatening retinopathy was found in 1.4% against 1.7% over 2 years, and the individualised arm needed 43.2% fewer appointments.
What London's records added

Pitt and colleagues took North East London's records from 2012 to 2023, when everyone was still invited yearly, and found 105,083 people with 2 clear screens. Over a mean of 5 years, 3,694 developed sight-threatening retinopathy, meaning a screening grade of R2, R3 or M1. The paper does not say how many were proliferative. Replaying the records on a 2-year cycle cut appointments by 54%, but 1,444 of those diagnoses, 39%, would have come a screen later.

The risk was uneven before the interval changed. Against the lowest-risk group, white people aged 41 or over with diabetes for under 10 years, almost every group was significantly more likely to have a sight-threatening diagnosis at an appointment: South Asian people 1.61 to 3.12 times, Black people 2.27 to 4.10, highest at 40 or under. The ratios were much the same with yearly screening, but a 2-year gap lets more build up: for Black people, the chance at each appointment rose from 0.8% to 2.4%, against 1% for the lowest-risk group. A points score using age, diabetes duration and ethnicity cut delayed diagnoses to 25% while saving 43% of appointments, and from 34% to 22% when tested on South East London's records.
Why it matters in practice

[The College of Optometrists' guidance](https://www.college-optometrists.org/clinical-guidance/guidance/knowledge,-skills-and-performance/examining-patients-with-diabetes-mellitus) covers the year between screens:

items: Ask whether the patient is in a screening programme and when they last attended, and say if you think it is overdue.
Keep sight-test recall as for someone without diabetes, whatever their screening interval, but use your judgement for younger people and people of Black and Asian ethnicities.
Dilating solely to look for retinopathy is not needed where a screening programme is in place.
Report relevant findings to whoever is responsible for the patient's care.

body.text: Beyond the guidance, record the result of the last screen as well as its date. Background retinopathy in someone on the 2-year cycle is a relevant finding to report, though a report does not by itself change their screening interval. Younger patients may matter twice: in London, people aged 40 or under were particularly at risk beyond 3 years, and a September review of 14 UK studies from 2006 to 2021 found younger age, in bands such as 12 to 39, and deprivation the most consistent markers of missed or late screening.
The caveats

items: The Four Nations study used 2005 to 2012 data, and its authors said the spread between programmes may partly reflect grading.
London's 39% is a simulation on yearly-screening records, so it cannot show how people respond to fewer invitations.
ISDR tested a clinical-data calculator, not England's rule, in one programme whose participants were 94.6% white, over 2 years.
The points score needs recorded ethnicity, which some programmes hold incompletely.
London's funders were Wellcome, the Health Foundation, the NHS Transformation Directorate and the NIHR. Its authors also research automated grading, covered on [our news page](/news).

seo.metaDescription: Diabetic retinopathy and driving: the DVLA's 120° field rule, why eyes lose field without laser, and what optometrists should record.
seo.metaTitle: Diabetic retinopathy and driving: DVLA rules after laser

keyPoints: Car and motorcycle drivers must report retinopathy lasered in both eyes, or the only eye with sight, and the DVLA's guidance for clinicians adds bilateral retinopathy with a field defect.
On a binocular Esterman, a car licence needs 120° wide, 50° each side and no significant defect within 20° of fixation. Bus and lorry: 160°, 70° each side and a clear central 30°.
In a re-analysis of the 1970s Diabetic Retinopathy Study, untreated eyes with severe retinopathy had lost about as much field as lasered ones by year 3.
Record whether the patient drives, which eye has had laser or injections, any abnormal field printout, and the advice given, including their legal duty to tell the DVLA.

faq.a: You can if you meet the visual standards for driving, but some drivers with it must tell the DVLA. Car and motorcycle drivers in Great Britain must report diabetic retinopathy treated with laser in both eyes, or in the only eye with sight, and bus and lorry drivers in either eye. The DVLA's guidance for clinicians also makes bilateral retinopathy with a field defect notifiable. The DVLA may then refer them for an eyesight test, and it decides on the licence. Anyone told by an optician, GP or eye specialist that they should not drive must also tell the DVLA.
faq.q: Can you drive if you have diabetic retinopathy?

faq.a: The binocular Esterman test is done with both eyes open, and it is the method the DVLA normally requires when it needs a field assessment for driving. To be reliable for licensing the false-positive score must be no more than 20%. For a car or motorcycle licence the field must be at least 120° on the horizontal, extending at least 50° to each side, with no significant defect within 20° of fixation above or below the horizontal. A bus or lorry licence needs at least 160° and 70° to each side, with no defect within the central 30°.
faq.q: What is an Esterman visual field test?

faq.a: The patient is legally responsible for telling the DVLA (the DVA in Northern Ireland). The College of Optometrists' guidance is that an optometrist who thinks a patient is unfit to drive should tell them so, put the advice in writing and record it. If the patient keeps driving and cannot be persuaded to stop, the optometrist should contact the DVLA and tell the patient, and the College notes that the public interest can justify breaking confidentiality to do so.
faq.q: Do opticians report to the DVLA?

faq.a: It can. Scatter laser burns can cause peripheral field loss, and in the Diabetic Retinopathy Study lasered eyes lost field faster in the first months than untreated ones. But untreated severe retinopathy lost field too, and by year 3 the two were no longer significantly different. What the DVLA judges is whether the binocular field and the acuity still meet its standards.
faq.q: Does laser treatment for diabetic retinopathy affect your vision for driving?

body.text: On diabetic retinopathy and driving, the DVLA's public list is short: a car or motorcycle driver must report diabetic retinopathy "with laser treatment" in both eyes, or in the only eye with sight. A 2025 re-analysis of two landmark trials, funded by the US National Eye Institute and published in Ophthalmology Retina, found that untreated eyes with severe retinopathy had lost about as much field by year 3 as lasered eyes.
That matters at the sight test. The list names laser, not injections, and severe retinopathy narrowed the field without either.
Diabetic retinopathy and driving: what the DVLA asks

The [DVLA's guide for drivers](https://www.gov.uk/eye-conditions-and-driving/print) has a bus or lorry driver report it in either eye, on form V1V. The DVLA may refer a driver to its contracted optician for a free eyesight test. A test from another optician must include an Esterman visual test and may still not be accepted.

[Its guidance for clinicians](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/visual-disorders-assessing-fitness-to-drive), updated in September 2025, lists bilateral retinopathy among the disorders that produce a field defect: for car and motorcycle drivers, the DVLA must be notified and the field standard met, laser or not. That standard is at least 120° on the horizontal, 50° to each side, and no significant defect within 20° of fixation above or below the horizontal meridian, on a binocular Esterman with no more than 20% false positives. Four or more adjoining missed points within the central 20° are generally regarded as significant. A bus or lorry licence needs at least 160°, 70° to each side and 30° above and below, with no defect within the central 30°. Acuity, the number plate and 6/12, is a separate subject in [this series](/news).
What the field studies found

The [re-analysis](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13474406/) took 830 participants of the Diabetic Retinopathy Study (1972 to 1979), each with severe non-proliferative or proliferative retinopathy and one eye randomised to laser, the other to none. Goldmann fields were scored as the field's extent summed over 12 meridians: 900 at most, 729 on average at the start. Lasered eyes lost 54.6 of that score by 4 months, untreated eyes 21.5. The untreated eyes kept losing, and by year 3 the difference was no longer significant. At 5 years they were down 156.7, the lasered eyes 124.9.

In [Protocol S](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7042909/), a US trial in proliferative retinopathy, an exploratory analysis of the 167 eyes with usable fields at the start found that eyes on ranibizumab lost little field for 2 years, then lost it through year 5. At 5 years the total point score had fallen by 330 dB with ranibizumab and 527 dB with laser, and by about 200 in ranibizumab eyes when tests after any later laser were left out.

In Sweden, 15 of 27 people who lost their licences over field loss after laser passed a driving simulator test, though as a group they drove less safely than controls, and none of the 13 relicensed had an injury accident in 3 to 6 years, which the authors call uncertain with so few licences ([Eye, 2022](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9829869/)).
Why it matters in practice

The DVLA decides who is fit to drive. The optometrist controls the record and the advice, and [the College's guidance on records](https://www.college-optometrists.org/clinical-guidance/guidance/knowledge,-skills-and-performance/patient-records) asks for whether the patient drives, any field test with screener, programme and correction, a printout of any abnormal result, and the oral and written advice. For a patient with diabetes:

items: Ask whether they drive, on a car or a bus or lorry licence, since the rules differ, and which eye has had laser or injections. Write it down.

Laser to both eyes, or to the only eye with sight, must be reported by a car driver, online or on form V1, and laser to either eye by a bus or lorry driver, on form V1V. Under the clinicians' guidance, so is bilateral retinopathy with a field defect. Tell them, and record that you did.
Where retinopathy is severe or treated in both eyes, it would make sense to run a binocular Esterman, the DVLA's own test, if your screener has one. Keep any abnormal printout.

If they do not meet the standard, tell them they have a legal duty to inform the DVLA (the DVA in Northern Ireland), advise them not to drive, put it in writing and record it, as [the College's guidance on patients who drive](https://www.college-optometrists.org/clinical-guidance/guidance/knowledge,-skills-and-performance/examining-patients-who-drive) sets out. If they keep driving and cannot be persuaded to stop, it says to contact the DVLA and tell the patient.

body.text: The caveats

items: The Diabetic Retinopathy Study ran in the 1970s, with heavier burns, Goldmann fields and poorer control of glucose, blood pressure and cholesterol than now, its authors say.
The catch-up was in severe retinopathy: in the milder ETDRS eyes, lasered eyes had still lost more at 7 years, 203.9 against 79.2.
320 of the 830 untreated eyes were lasered on progressing and left the analysis, which the authors think understates untreated loss, and cataract or glaucoma may explain some decline.
Protocol S had 5-year fields for 79 of the 234 eyes in its field study.
None of the three measured a pass or fail against the UK standard.

seo.metaDescription: What the Diwali evidence says about the six hours after a firework eye injury, and the one question worth asking before you refer.
seo.metaTitle: Firework eye injury: what to ask before you refer

keyPoints: Eighty-one per cent of serious UK firework eye injuries reported to the BOSU fell in October and November. Bonfire Night and Diwali are three days apart in 2026.
In 67 patients over two Diwali periods at three Indian centres, the median time from injury to presentation was six hours and 82.1% were closed-globe.
A population survey of 2,160 adults in rural Haryana found 25.7% used a home remedy in the eye, and 14 of the 85 who had had an ocular injury, 16.4%, had used one for it.
The harm runs through contamination and delay, not through anything exotic. The question to ask is what has already gone in the eye, and it belongs on every referral, not on some of them.

faq.a: Do not let anything else go into the eye, and do not wait to see whether it settles. In the British Ophthalmological Surveillance Unit's two-year study of serious UK firework eye injuries, 53% of the 47 patients needed ocular surgery, 17% lost the eye to enucleation or evisceration, and 53% of those followed up were 6/60 or worse at six months. A shield rather than a pad, nothing instilled, and the same-day eye casualty.
faq.q: What should you do for a firework eye injury?

faq.a: The British Ophthalmological Surveillance Unit asked every ophthalmologist in the UK to report serious firework eye injuries every month for two years from July 2004 and collected 47 cases. Eighty-one per cent fell in October and November and 27% were in people under 18. That is the last national surveillance of its kind, so the figure is a floor for serious injury rather than a current count.
faq.q: How common are firework eye injuries in the UK?

faq.a: No, and the reason is not that the remedy is unusual. A population-based survey of 2,160 adults in rural Haryana found that of the 529 who used a home remedy in the eye, 61.4% used kajal, 31.4% honey, 11.7% ghee and 9.1% rose water. The authors attribute the harm to two ordinary mechanisms: contamination of a surface that is already broken, and the delay that comes from trying something before seeking care.
faq.q: Is it safe to put kajal, honey or rose water in an injured eye?

faq.a: Not all of them. In the Indian multicentre series of 67 patients, 65.7% were handling the firework themselves and 34.3% were bystanders. The bystander share matters in the chair: a third of the people who present were not doing anything, which is worth remembering before asking how it happened.
faq.q: Do most firework eye injuries happen to the person holding the firework?

body.text: Eighty-one per cent of the serious firework eye injuries reported to the [British Ophthalmological Surveillance Unit](https://www.nature.com/articles/6702778) happened in October and November. In 2026 the two nights that fill those months are three days apart: Bonfire Night on Thursday 5 November, Diwali on Sunday the 8th.

The BOSU study ran for two years from July 2004. Every ophthalmologist in the UK was sent a card each month and asked to report any new serious firework eye injury, or to confirm there had been none. Forty-seven cases came back. Twenty-six per cent had a penetrating injury. Fifty-three per cent needed ocular surgery. Eight patients, 17%, lost the eye to enucleation or evisceration, and four more needed a cosmetic shell for phthisis. At six months, 53% of those followed up were 6/60 or worse. Twenty-seven per cent were under 18.
That is the national picture and it is twenty years old. A study published this August adds the one number the UK data never had.
Six hours

A [multicentre prospective study](https://doi.org/10.4103/ijo.ijo_2784_25) followed 67 consecutive patients with firecracker eye injuries through the Diwali periods of 2023 and 2024, at three tertiary centres in Central and Western India. Children were 62.7% of them and males 89.6%. Two-thirds, 65.7%, were handling the firework themselves; the other 34.3% were watching. Blast was the mechanism in 80.6% and 82.1% of the injuries were closed-globe. More than 40% presented with acuity worse than 6/60 and 23.9% needed surgery.
The median time from injury to presentation was six hours.
Only the abstract is published. The paper is ahead of print and not deposited anywhere open, so nothing above goes further than what the abstract states.
What fills the six hours
Nobody sits for six hours with an injured eye doing nothing.

A [population-based survey](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0183461) interviewed 2,160 adults across 25 rural clusters in Haryana and asked, among other things, what they put in their eyes. Of the 2,055 asked about home remedies, 529 (25.7%) had used one. Kajal accounted for 61.4% of those, honey 31.4%, ghee 11.7% and rose water 9.1%.

The number that matters here is smaller and more specific. Eighty-five of the people interviewed had sustained an ocular injury. Fourteen of them, 16.4%, had used a traditional eye medicine for it. Thirty-five, 41.2%, had sought no treatment at all.

The authors' argument is not that kajal is exotic. It is that the harm runs through two ordinary mechanisms: contamination of a surface that is already broken, and the delay that comes from trying something first.
The limitations of the firework eye injury evidence

That survey was done in rural North India and published in 2017, in a population with a mean age of 55.6 where two-thirds had primary schooling or less. It does not describe a UK high street. I could not find a survey of what patients here put in an injured eye before they arrive, and that is the honest gap in this piece.

What transfers is the shape of the behaviour rather than the contents of the cupboard. Reaching for something at home before reaching for a professional is not a regional habit, and the two mechanisms do not care what was reached for. The pathway argument is the same one [Denmark's high street OCT data](/news/denmark-oct-teleophthalmology-referrals) made from the other end: what the high street can see matters less than what happens next.
Why it matters in practice

items: Ask what has already gone in the eye. Ask it of everyone, in the same words, before you ask anything else, and ask it without a face that makes the answer harder to give.
Time is the variable you can change. Six hours was the median in a series where more than 40% arrived worse than 6/60; the delay is the mechanism, not the remedy on its own.
A quiet eye is not a reassuring one. Closed-globe injuries were 82.1% of the Diwali series, and a closed globe is what walks into a practice rather than an eye casualty.
A third of them were bystanders. 34.3% of that series were watching, not handling, which is worth remembering before the history starts with what they were doing.

seo.metaTitle: Halloween contact lenses: UK law and the risks

keyPoints: In a 2023 check, only 6 of 47 websites selling cosmetic lenses met section 27 of the Opticians Act 1989, which says who may sell a zero powered contact lens.
In a survey of 3,803 women in Japan, buying lenses online or in a shop rather than from an eye clinic was associated with more self-reported eye problems needing care.
Cosmetic and clear lens wearers in Japan reported such problems about as often, but in an Asian hospital study Acanthamoeba caused 9% of cosmetic lens infections, against 1% of the others.
No UK count of costume lens infections after Halloween could be found.

faq.a: Yes, if they are sold as the law requires. Under section 27 of the Opticians Act 1989, a zero powered contact lens may only be sold by or under the supervision of a registered medical practitioner, a registered optometrist or a registered dispensing optician, and the seller must make arrangements for aftercare. Giving lenses away free still counts as selling them. When 47 websites selling cosmetic lenses were checked against section 27 in February 2023, only 6 met its requirements.
faq.q: Are Halloween contact lenses legal in the UK?

faq.a: No study here looks separately at costume lenses worn for one night. In a survey of 3,803 women in Japan, cosmetic lens wearers were about as likely as clear lens wearers to report needing eye care for a lens problem in the previous year (35.7% against 33.4%). The survey did not measure infections. Buying lenses online or in a shop rather than from an eye clinic was associated with more such reports. In an Asian hospital study, Acanthamoeba caused 9% of infections in cosmetic lens wearers, against 1% in other lens wearers.
faq.q: Are Halloween contact lenses safe?

faq.a: Yes. The authors of a 2026 UK study call contact lens wear the predominant risk factor for Pseudomonas keratitis in developed countries. They cite studies linking lens wear to microtrauma, intermittent hypoxia and contamination from water or lens cases, all of which help the bacteria into the cornea. In Birmingham and Nottingham, 35 of 66 culture-proven Pseudomonas keratitis cases were in lens wearers, and 94.3% of those ended with a corrected distance visual acuity of 6/24 or better. In 861 severe keratitis admissions in Toulouse, lens wear was the commonest risk factor, present in 32.2%, and was associated with Gram-negative bacilli such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
faq.q: Can contact lenses cause keratitis?

body.text: In [a February 2023 check](https://doi.org/10.1097/ICL.0000000000001080), only 6 of 47 websites selling cosmetic contact lenses complied with [section 27 of the Opticians Act 1989](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1989/44/section/27). Section 27 allows a zero powered contact lens to be sold only by or under the supervision of a registered medical practitioner, a registered optometrist or a registered dispensing optician.

No study here looks at Halloween contact lenses as such. In [a web survey of 3,803 women in Japan](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-95318-7), buying lenses online or in a shop rather than from an eye clinic or hospital was associated with more self-reported eye problems needing care.
What the Japanese survey did

In November 2018, a market research company surveyed 4,000 lens-wearing women aged 16 to 49, chosen at random from its Japanese panel. Of the 3,803 analysed, 1,833 wore cosmetic lenses (colour-enhancing, opaque or limbal circle) and 1,970 wore clear lenses. They reported where they bought lenses, how they wore them, and whether tearing, pain or blurred vision from a lens had sent them for eye care in the previous year. Japan's medical research agency funded it, and one author declared contact lens industry funding outside the work.
What it found

Cosmetic and clear lens wearers reported a problem about as often (35.7% against 33.4%), and lens type was not associated with problems before or after adjustment (adjusted odds ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.11). Compared with buying from an eye clinic or hospital, buying online was associated with more problems (adjusted odds ratio 1.23, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.45), and so was buying in a shop (1.28, 1.06 to 1.54). So were replacing lenses late (1.53) and sleeping in them (1.25). Half the cosmetic lens wearers bought online (50.9%, against 25.3% of clear lens wearers).
Who presents with a cosmetic lens infection

Over 12 months at 11 centres in eight Asian countries, cosmetic lens wearers made up 204 of 694 patients with a contact lens corneal infection (29.4%). They were more often female (90% against 59%) and under 25 (68% against 44%), and newer to lenses. Presenting disease and visual outcomes were similar in both groups, but Acanthamoeba caused 9% of the cosmetic lens infections, against 1% of the others.

In a smaller French study in 12 university hospitals from 2007 to 2009, 32 of 256 patients with a contact lens infection (12.5%) had worn cosmetic lenses, rarely dispensed by eye care professionals. Final acuity was worse than 20/200 in 60% of the cosmetic lens cases, against 13% of the others. These two studies and the website check are open only as abstracts, and nothing here goes beyond them.

In Birmingham and Nottingham from 2016 to 2020, 35 of 66 culture-proven Pseudomonas keratitis cases were in contact lens wearers. Of those, 94.3% ended with a corrected distance visual acuity of 6/24 or better, which the authors say was likely due to milder disease at presentation and timely management.

I found no UK count of costume lens infections around Halloween. In a series of 861 severe keratitis admissions in Toulouse from 2016 to 2021, published in September 2026, contact lens cases peaked in summer: 103 of 277, against 63 in autumn.
What UK law says about Halloween contact lenses

Giving a lens away still counts as selling it, and the seller must make arrangements for the wearer to receive aftercare, in so far as and for so long as is reasonable. Selling in breach of the supervision rule can bring a fine of up to level 5 on the standard scale. In the 2023 check, 13 of 49 brands on sale (26.5%) had no CE marking.
Why it matters in practice

items: Ask a young patient with a red eye about coloured or costume lenses by name. In both hospital studies, cosmetic lens wearers were younger and newer to lenses, and I suspect a pair worn for one night is easy to leave out of a history.
Ask where the lenses came from and how they were worn, including whether they were slept in.

Treat a painful red eye in a costume lens wearer as contact lens keratitis until shown otherwise, with Acanthamoeba on the list. The Midlands authors think timely management helped their patients, and [this week's piece on firework eye injuries](/news) makes the same case for early care.

Tell parents to buy costume lenses only where the sale is made by or under the supervision of a registered medical practitioner, a registered optometrist or a registered dispensing optician. A lens that leaves an eye red and painful should come out, and the eye should be seen that day.

body.text: The caveats

items: The Japanese survey is cross-sectional and self-reported, in women recruited online, with no data on lens brands. A problem meant seeking eye care, not a confirmed infection.

Its categories (eye clinic or hospital, shop, internet) do not match the UK's line between supervised and unsupervised sale. Its authors warned that counterfeit cosmetic lenses could harm young women disproportionately.
The French and Asian studies report outcomes differently, so the contrast is only suggestive.
Neither 2026 study separates cosmetic lenses, and Toulouse counted only severe cases admitted to one hospital.

seo.metaDescription: Two UK trials tested starting glaucoma eye drops against laser and surgery. Both found less field loss without drops, and patients who felt no difference.
seo.metaTitle: Glaucoma eye drops, laser or surgery first?

keyPoints: In TAGS, 453 adults with newly diagnosed advanced glaucoma were randomised to primary trabeculectomy or to drops. At five years their quality of life was the same: VFQ-25 83.3 against 81.3.
Their clinical outcomes were not. Visual field mean deviation was –14.30 dB with surgery against –16.74 dB with drops, and IOP 12.07 against 14.76 mmHg. Safety events: 52.2% and 57.9%.
In LiGHT at six years, 69.8% of eyes started on laser were at or below target pressure with no drops or surgery, and fewer progressed than on drops: 19.6% against 26.8%.
One year of first-line drops in 88 treatment-naive eyes thinned the corneal epithelium from 45.6 to 43.9 µm, cut break-up time from 8.3 to 6.9 seconds and nearly doubled OSDI, 7.3 to 13.4.

faq.a: They change it measurably within a year. In a 2026 prospective study of 88 treatment-naive eyes, one year of first-line therapy thinned the total epithelial thickness from 45.6 to 43.9 µm, shortened tear break-up time from 8.3 to 6.9 seconds, thinned the lipid layer from 3.8 to 3.0 nm and raised the OSDI score from 7.3 to 13.4. Total corneal thickness did not change significantly. The study followed one cohort on the Colombian Caribbean coast for twelve months, so it describes the first year of treatment rather than the long run.
faq.q: Do glaucoma drops damage the ocular surface?

faq.a: On the measures clinicians treat by, the LiGHT trial found it was. At six years, 69.8% of eyes started on selective laser trabeculoplasty were still at or below their target pressure with no drops and no surgery, and 19.6% had progressed against 26.8% of eyes started on drops (p = 0.006). On the measures patients report (EQ-5D-5L, the Glaucoma Utility Index and GQL-15) there was no significant difference at all.
faq.q: Is laser better than drops for newly diagnosed glaucoma?

faq.a: TAGS is the trial that tested it. In 453 adults with newly diagnosed advanced open-angle glaucoma, primary trabeculectomy gave lower pressure (12.07 vs 14.76 mmHg) and less field loss at five years (mean deviation –14.30 vs –16.74 dB) than starting on drops, with no excess of safety events (52.2% vs 57.9%, relative risk 0.92). Vision-related quality of life was the same in both arms. The decision belongs to the glaucoma service, but the referral is where the case for it is made.
faq.q: Should advanced glaucoma go straight to surgery?

body.text: Almost every newly diagnosed patient starts on glaucoma eye drops. Two long UK trials tested what happens when they do not. In the Treatment of Advanced Glaucoma Study, at five years, the patients randomised to surgery and the patients randomised to drops rated their own vision almost identically: 83.3 out of 100 on the 25-item Visual Function Questionnaire against 81.3, a difference of 1.01 with a confidence interval running from –1.99 to 4.00. On the trial’s primary outcome, there was nothing in it.

Their visual fields were not identical. Mean deviation was –14.30 dB in the surgery arm and –16.74 dB in the medication arm, a difference of 1.87 dB that did not straddle zero (95% CI 0.87 to 2.87). Pressures were 12.07 mmHg against 14.76. Safety events, the worry with a primary trabeculectomy, occurred in 52.2% of the surgery arm and 57.9% of the medication arm, a relative risk of 0.92, which is to say no signal of extra harm.

[TAGS](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ophtha.2024.01.007) recruited 453 adults with newly diagnosed advanced open-angle glaucoma from 27 UK secondary care departments. It answers the question an optometrist actually faces when a field comes back badly damaged at first presentation: does it matter what this patient is started on?
The same shape at the other end of severity

[LiGHT](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ophtha.2022.09.009) asked the same question for newly diagnosed ocular hypertension and early glaucoma, with selective laser trabeculoplasty as the alternative to drops. At six years, 633 of the 692 patients who finished the first three years entered the extension and 524 completed. Quality of life came out level again: no significant difference on the EQ-5D-5L, the Glaucoma Utility Index or the GQL-15.

The clinical numbers did not come out level. Just under seven in ten eyes started on laser, 69.8%, were still at or below target pressure at six years with no drops and no surgery. And more eyes progressed in the drops arm than the laser arm: 26.8% against 19.6%, p = 0.006.
What a year of drops does to a surface that has never seen them

The ocular surface case against chronic drops is usually argued from patients who have been on them for years, which makes it hard to separate the drug from the disease from the decade. A [2026 prospective study](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10792-025-03612-4) took 88 eyes of 44 treatment-naive patients and measured them before and after a year of first-line therapy.

Total corneal thickness barely moved, from 537.6 to 533.8 µm, and that change was not significant. The epithelium did: total epithelial thickness fell from 45.6 to 43.9 µm, and that one was. Tear break-up time dropped from 8.3 to 6.9 seconds, the lipid layer from 3.8 to 3.0 nm, and OSDI nearly doubled, 7.3 to 13.4.
None of that is catastrophic in a year. All of it is the first year of what may be thirty.
Where glaucoma eye drops actually sit

The ocular surface argument is real, and measurable inside twelve months in eyes that had nothing wrong with them. It is not, on its own, the argument for laser or surgery first. That argument is progression: 19.6% against 26.8% in LiGHT, 1.87 dB in TAGS. The surface is why a patient stops taking the drops, which is a different problem and just as important.

Patients on drops and patients who avoided them rate their vision the same. The person in front of you has no way of feeling 1.87 dB. That makes the case for offering laser first an entirely clinical one, and it puts the job of making it on whoever is holding the fields, which, increasingly, is the high street. The Danish pathway in [what putting OCT into 79 optician stores did to referrals](/news/denmark-oct-teleophthalmology-referrals) is the same argument from the other end.
The limitations worth carrying into clinic

TAGS randomised people whose glaucoma was already advanced when it was found, so its result does not transfer to every new diagnosis. LiGHT randomised the opposite end: treatment-naive ocular hypertension and early glaucoma. Neither asked what happens to someone already established on drops, which is most of the patients an optometrist sees. The ocular surface figures are one cohort of 44 patients followed for a year; they show what the first year does, not the tenth.
Why it matters in practice

items: A newly diagnosed patient who asks whether they have to be on drops for life now has a real answer: in LiGHT, seven in ten eyes started on laser were still controlled at six years without them.

A patient already on drops who reports grittiness, fluctuating vision or a short break-up time is describing something the trials measured at one year in eyes with no prior disease. It is worth recording, and worth saying in the referral.
A field that is already advanced at first presentation is the TAGS population. The referral letter that says so is the one that gets the conversation about primary surgery started.
Neither trial says drops are wrong. Both say the choice is worth making deliberately rather than by default.

seo.metaDescription: Microperimetry, acuity or scans? Why Europe refused a GA drug the US approved on lesion growth, and what 87 eyes in a 2026 study add for practice.
seo.metaTitle: Microperimetry vs visual acuity: what regulators accept

keyPoints: The US approved pegcetacoplan for geographic atrophy in 2023 on lesion growth: 0.70 to 0.87 mm² less than the 4 mm² with sham over 24 months (17% to 22%), in trials of 1,258 patients.
Europe refused it in 2024: no prespecified measure of function, acuity and microperimetry included, showed a meaningful difference or trend. The MHRA's UK rejection was reported in 2025.
In early atrophic AMD (87 eyes), lesion size tracked microperimetry and acuity the distance from the fovea. In 102 mostly late AMD patients, better-eye acuity tracked daily function more closely.
Acuity is not being retired: ARCHER II, a phase 3 trial in geographic atrophy, is judged on a loss of 15 letters or more.

faq.a: Microperimetry presents spots of light of varying brightness onto the retina at points centred on the fovea, measures the faintest each point can see, and tracks the retina so the same points are tested at every visit. It tests the macula around the fovea, which acuity does not. Experts advising the European Medicines Agency called it the best available test of retinal function in geographic atrophy, though it is not clear how much change in it patients notice. In a 2026 Utah study it tracked the size of early atrophy more closely than acuity did.
faq.q: What is microperimetry?

faq.a: For how patients manage day to day, acuity still leads: in a Dutch study of 102 AMD patients, most with late AMD, acuity in the better-seeing eye explained more of their daily visual functioning than mesopic microperimetry did. It is weakest early, while atrophy spares the fovea, which is why geographic atrophy trials measured lesion growth on scans. The US approved pegcetacoplan on that. Europe accepted lesion growth as the main measure but would not approve without at least a positive trend in visual function, and ARCHER II, a phase 3 trial, is judged on letters lost.
faq.q: Is visual acuity still the gold standard?

faq.a: Syfovre (pegcetacoplan) slowed the growth of geographic atrophy on autofluorescence over 24 months in two trials that randomised 1,258 patients, and the US approved it in 2023. The European Medicines Agency refused it in 2024: none of the prespecified measures of function, including acuity, reading speed and microperimetry, showed a meaningful difference or a positive trend, set against the risks of regular injections, including wet AMD, inflammation and endophthalmitis. The Macular Society reported in January 2025 that the MHRA had rejected it for the UK, concerned about whether it meaningfully improved patients' ability to see and manage daily tasks.
faq.q: Why was Syfovre refused in Europe and the UK?

faq.a: Low luminance acuity is the ETDRS chart read through a 2.0 log unit neutral density filter, which lowers the light 100 times. The Vision Academy recommends it alongside standard acuity, especially in dry AMD, as a simple, inexpensive and relatively rapid test, though testing is not yet standardised. In a 2026 Utah study of early atrophy it followed distance from the fovea, as standard acuity did.
faq.q: What is low luminance visual acuity?

body.text: The US approved pegcetacoplan, the first drug for geographic atrophy, in February 2023 on scans showing slower lesion growth. [The European Medicines Agency's assessment report](https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/assessment-report/syfovre-epar-refusal-public-assessment-report_en.pdf) explains why Europe refused it: over 24 months no prespecified measure of function, acuity and microperimetry included, showed a meaningful difference or even a positive trend to weigh against the risks of regular injections. The MHRA's UK rejection was reported in January 2025.

Chart and scan disagree earlier in the disease too. [A study published in September in the American Journal of Ophthalmology](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajo.2026.09.029) suggests why: in early atrophic AMD, with lesions far smaller than the trials', acuity tracked distance from the fovea and microperimetry tracked lesion size.
What the trials measured

OAKS and DERBY randomised 1,258 patients with geographic atrophy of 2.5 to 17.5 mm² to pegcetacoplan monthly or every other month, or sham, for 24 months, measured on fundus autofluorescence. [The FDA's label](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2023/217171s000lbl.pdf) gives modelled growth over 24 months of 3.98 mm² with sham in OAKS and 4.00 mm² in DERBY, and 0.70 to 0.87 mm² less with pegcetacoplan, 17.4% to 21.9% slower.

Every key secondary endpoint measured function: acuity, reading speed, a reading-independence index and, in OAKS only, microperimetry. None showed a meaningful difference or a positive trend. A late, post hoc OCT analysis found photoreceptor loss slowing even more. The committee's answer:
the observed reduction of the GA lesion growth rate (regardless of the specific measurement) remains an anatomical endpoint that can in itself not demonstrate clinically relevant patient benefit.
What the US and Europe each accepted

Europe had agreed lesion area could be the primary measure if the trials showed at least a positive trend in visual function. Its experts, in June 2024, called lesion size an acceptable primary outcome and microperimetry the best available test of retinal function in geographic atrophy, with acuity measured but not as the primary endpoint. The committee accepted that acuity can miss loss while the fovea is spared, but acuity fell 6.94 letters over two years with sham, so a real effect should at least have shown as a trend.

It refused by majority, weighing the missing benefit against the risks of regular injections, including wet AMD, inflammation and endophthalmitis. Eleven members dissented: with the fovea spared so long, a benefit may not have been possible to show within the trials, and post hoc microperimetry showed the preserved retina still responded to light. The majority judged them inconsistent between doses, at around one scotomatous point.

The FDA has also approved a treatment on an OCT primary endpoint. [Encelto's label](https://www.fda.gov/media/185726/download), for macular telangiectasia type 2, gives the rate of ellipsoid zone loss on SD-OCT over 24 months: 0.075 against 0.166 mm² with sham in one trial, 0.111 against 0.160 in the other. Its secondary microperimetry endpoint differed in the first (p = 0.02), not the second (p = 0.83).
Microperimetry and acuity in early atrophy

The Utah study took 87 eyes with early atrophic AMD, lesions no larger than 1.27 mm². In the 38 with atrophy on autofluorescence, each doubling of lesion size went with 3.55 dB lower mesopic sensitivity on microperimetry aimed at the lesion. Acuity, low luminance acuity and reading followed distance from the fovea, about 4 to 5 letters per mm for acuity, with no consistent link to lesion size. We could read only its abstract, and nothing here goes beyond it.

In [a Dutch study of 102 AMD patients](https://doi.org/10.1167/tvst.15.2.5), most with late AMD in at least one eye, acuity in the better-seeing eye explained 38% of the variation in daily visual functioning, and adding mesopic microperimetry on a fixed 37-point grid raised that only to 46%. The authors suggest acuity gives stronger evidence of clinical efficacy.
Why it matters in practice

items: A 6/6 beside atrophy on the OCT is consistent with a spared fovea, not proof of one, and says nothing about the atrophy's size. Check the fovea on the OCT and record how far the atrophy sits from it.

[The Vision Academy's consensus](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00417-023-06272-1) recommends low luminance acuity alongside standard acuity: the ETDRS chart through a 2.0 log unit neutral density filter, simple, inexpensive and relatively rapid, though not yet standardised. In the Utah eyes it followed the fovea too.

A patient asking about the US injections for geographic atrophy can be told the first was refused in Europe and the UK: no benefit to sight was shown to set against the risks of injections. [Our interactive simulation of dry AMD](/vision) shows its stages.

[ARCHER II](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06510816), a phase 3 trial of vonaprument in 659 patients, is judged on the proportion losing 15 letters or more by month 15, with primary completion estimated for October 2026.

body.text: The caveats

items: Both regulators accepted that the drug slowed lesion growth. Europe's final assessment covered every other month dosing only, monthly dosing having been dropped over adverse events.
DERBY narrowly missed its prespecified 12-month primary endpoint. The difference was larger at 24 months, but that was not the prespecified test.
The Utah and Dutch studies are cross-sectional, with different patients and microperimetry methods.
The Vision Academy is funded by Bayer, and Bayer part-funded the Dutch study.

seo.metaDescription: The number plate eye test is a daylight test. With contrast cut too, a 6/12 cut-off caught 61% of plate failures near it, against 97% for blur alone.
seo.metaTitle: Number plate eye test: what it misses at night

keyPoints: The UK standard: a number plate read in good daylight at 20 metres, 6/12 and the minimum field of vision. DVLA cataract guidance says glare may stop a driver passing even when acuity looks adequate.
Near the cut-off, a 6/12 chart caught 61% of plate failures when glasses cut contrast too, against 97% in the same team's earlier study of blur alone, in other people.
In a night-driving simulator, contrast sensitivity and low-contrast acuity tracked hazard detection in drivers aged 55 to 81; high-contrast acuity did not (P = 0.10, 21 measurements from 15 drivers).
In 144 drivers aged 70 and over from US eye clinics, none had acuity worse than 6/12 and 18.8% had impaired contrast sensitivity, not significantly linked to daylight on-road scores.

faq.a: It is the practical half of the UK Group 1 driving vision standard: reading a registration mark in good daylight at 20 metres on a car registered since 1 September 2001, or 20.5 metres for an older plate. It is not the whole standard. A driver also needs visual acuity of at least Snellen 6/12 with both eyes open and a minimum field of vision. DVLA, not the optometrist, decides whether someone is medically fit to drive.
faq.q: What is the number plate eye test and how far away is it?

faq.a: Not necessarily. The plate test is done in good daylight on high-contrast characters. In a night-driving simulator, high-contrast acuity was not significantly associated with how early drivers aged 55 to 81 detected a hazard (r = 0.37, P = 0.10, 21 measurements from 15 drivers), while contrast sensitivity and low-contrast acuity were. Meeting the standard is a legal minimum, not a statement about driving at night.
faq.q: Does passing the number plate test mean your eyesight is good enough for night driving?

faq.a: Acuity is the smallest high-contrast letter you can read. Contrast sensitivity is the faintest difference between light and dark you can still see, which is closer to what night driving asks of an eye: a pedestrian in dark clothing, a kerb in the rain, a road lit by somebody else's headlights. It falls in cataract, which the College of Optometrists names alongside blur and glare as affecting driving, particularly at night. The site also has [a simulation of dry AMD at each stage](/vision), a different condition from the ones this piece is about.
faq.q: What is contrast sensitivity?

faq.a: In practice, with a Pelli-Robson chart at one metre, scored letter by letter. There is no contrast-sensitivity threshold in UK driving law, and the College of Optometrists says the evidence is not there to say which tests and cut-offs would be better, so the result is information for the conversation about night driving, glare and lenses rather than a pass or a fail.
faq.q: How do you test contrast sensitivity?

body.text: The clocks go back on Sunday 25 October and the night-driving conversation starts in every practice. The standard drivers are held to is the number plate eye test: a plate read in good daylight at 20 metres, plus acuity of at least 6/12. When Anglia Ruskin cut acuity and contrast together with simulation glasses in young volunteers, a Snellen 6/12 cut-off caught 61% of plate failures near the cut-off, against 97% in their earlier study of uncorrected blur.
The daylight in that standard is not decoration: in a night-driving simulator, contrast sensitivity tracked how early older drivers saw a hazard, and high-contrast acuity fell short of significance.
What the number plate eye test actually measures

[DVLA's guidance](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/visual-disorders-assessing-fitness-to-drive) sets the plate in good daylight at 20 metres, with Snellen 6/12 and a minimum field of vision on top. It writes the gap down itself, under cataract:
Glare may counter an ability to pass the number plate test of the minimum requirements, even when cataracts allow apparently appropriate acuities.
Where the chair stops predicting the kerb

Anglia Ruskin ran it twice, in two groups. First, in [a study in the British Journal of Ophthalmology](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjophthalmol-2014-306173), 120 staff and students read charts indoors uncorrected, then a real plate outdoors: in the uncertain band, 6/9 to 6/36, a 6/12 cut-off caught 97% of the failures. Then, in [the study published in Eye](https://doi.org/10.1038/eye.2015.188), 62 adults of mean age 25 wore simulation glasses that cut acuity and contrast sensitivity together, closer to cataract than to an old prescription. In its own band, 6/12 to 6/24, sensitivity fell to 61% and the false negatives, 6/12 in the chair and a fail at the kerb, rose from 2%, one person in 59, to 15%. Each is a proportion of its own band, not of all drivers.
What predicts hazard detection in the dark

[The night-driving evidence](https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2022.914459) comes from a simulator. Fifteen ophthalmologically healthy drivers aged 55 to 81 drove at obstacles of three contrasts while LED arrays on cable robots reproduced an oncoming car's dipped beams. Contrast sensitivity tracked the median distance at which a hazard was picked up, and low-contrast acuity at least as strongly. High-contrast acuity was not significantly associated (r = 0.37, P = 0.10), a null too small to trust. The headlights cut contrast sensitivity in 20 of 22 instances, a relative fall of 41%.
The study that cuts the other way

The largest of the driving studies, and the only one on real roads, found no significant association with daytime driving. In Alabama, 144 drivers aged 70 and over had a vision battery, then a 15-mile on-road drive scored by a masked driving rehabilitation specialist. None had acuity worse than 20/40, or 6/12, and 18.8% were impaired on Pelli-Robson, below 1.5 log sensitivity. That was not significantly associated with how they drove: the age-adjusted odds ratio for a worse score was 1.56 (95% CI 0.59 to 4.09), wide enough to hold a real effect. Only processing speed under divided attention and motion perception were associated. Every drive was in daylight, the authors say.
Why it matters in practice

There is no contrast-sensitivity threshold for car drivers in UK law, and [the College of Optometrists' position](https://www.college-optometrists.org/policy-and-influencing/position-statements/position-on-vision-standards-for-driving) is that the evidence is not there to say which tests and cut-offs would be better. The same statement says blur, glare and reduced contrast sensitivity, at night and in cataract, are known to affect driving and to raise the risk of at-fault and fatal collisions.

items: Use a logMAR chart such as an ETDRS, or a Snellen scored by full line. At 6/7.5 or better every participant in the blur study read the plate, but one in the contrast study failed it at +0.08 logMAR, so in cataract ask for a plate check too.
Ask anyone between 6/9 and 6/12 to read a plate at 20 metres themselves, in daylight. They pass the chart, and some cannot.
Measure contrast sensitivity where it changes the conversation: early cataract, or the patient whose acuity is fine and whose nights are not. It is information, not a legal test.
College guidance says an anti-reflection coating improves transmission, and that a sunglass tint passing under 75% of the light is not for road use in twilight or at night.

The DVLA, or the DVA in Northern Ireland, decides medical fitness and the patient must tell it. Advise them not to drive, put it in writing, record it, and if they will not stop, tell them you will notify the agency, then do so and tell them you have.

body.text: That last step is the one optometrists are least comfortable with. In [the GOC's 2026 registrant survey](https://optical.org/asset/CBD32D15%2D651E%2D4446%2DB973611110032D55/), 91% of optometrists had told a patient in the past year that they were no longer fit to drive, but only 32% would be comfortable telling the DVLA themselves if the patient would not, and 96% of all registrants who answered had not done so that year. Of all those uncomfortable, 72% named breaching confidentiality, which [the College's guidance](https://www.college-optometrists.org/clinical-guidance/guidance/knowledge,-skills-and-performance/examining-patients-who-drive) says the public interest can override when a driver rejects advice not to drive.
The caveats

items: Simulation glasses on 62 adults of mean age 25 are not cataract in older drivers.
The night-driving result is 15 healthy volunteers in one simulator. Several authors declare industry ties, and the German Social Accident Insurance funded it.
The Alabama drivers came from eye clinics, so 18.8% is not a population figure, and vision was tested six months before.
The night-driving authors are explicit that their own data do not speak directly to the real-world value of routinely testing night vision.
The GOC figures are self-reported by the 3,451 registrants who answered, an 11% response rate.

body.text: The number plate eye test is not a bad test. It is a daylight test, and it was never meant to answer the question that arrives in the last week of October.

seo.metaDescription: What an independent prescribing optometrist is paid to treat on the NHS in Scotland, what England commissions, and what Greater Manchester's data show.
seo.metaTitle: Independent prescribing optometrist: Scotland vs England

keyPoints: In Scotland, an approved independent prescribing optometrist or ophthalmic medical practitioner is paid £97.69 for a first appointment for an anterior eye condition: 10,267 claims by March 2026.
In May 2025 the College of Optometrists said community minor and urgent eye care, with or without prescribing, was available in 73% of England.
In Greater Manchester, under 1 in 100 cases in 2024 were prescribing cases. Looking back at 120 urgent referrals, hospital optometrists judged that a prescriber might have managed 40% in practice.
In the GOC's 2026 survey, 25% of 276 working registrants in Scotland felt under commercial pressure, against 32% of 2,252 in England, but 66% felt unable to cope with workload, against 58%.

faq.a: Optometrists with the additional independent prescribing qualification can prescribe licensed medicine for conditions affecting the eye and the tissues around it, within their competence. In Scotland they are given NHS prescription pads, and 674 were on health board lists at 31 March 2026. In England, NHS prescribing by independent prescribing (IP) optometrists depends on local commissioning: in Greater Manchester's urgent eyecare service in 2024, IP optometrists used their prescribing qualification in 460 cases, 0.8% of the total.
faq.q: Can optometrists prescribe medication in the UK?

faq.a: The General Ophthalmic Services (GOS) Specialist Supplementary service is a tier of the NHS eye examination in Scotland for ten anterior eye conditions, such as anterior uveitis and herpes simplex keratitis. It began on 1 August 2025 and was fully in place from 19 January 2026. An IP optometrist or ophthalmic medical practitioner approved by their health board gives the second stage of treatment, and is paid £97.69 for the first appointment and £47.80 for each follow-up. The service needs an approved prescriber nearby: when the Scottish Government assessed it, Orkney had none. Public Health Scotland counted about 21,000 claims in 2025/26, 10,267 of them for first appointments.
faq.q: What is the GOS specialist supplementary service in Scotland?

faq.a: No. Community minor and urgent eye care services, run as the Community Urgent Eyecare Service (CUES) or the Minor Eye Conditions Service (MECS), are commissioned locally, with or without prescribing. In May 2025 the College of Optometrists said they were available in 73% of England, while every patient in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland had access. Where the service runs, people with red, itchy or painful eyes, minor eye injuries, flashes and floaters or sudden vision problems can be seen by a local optometrist without a GP referral.
faq.q: Is the minor eye conditions service available everywhere in England?

body.text: Since 19 January, an independent prescribing optometrist in Scotland who is approved by their health board can be paid by the NHS to treat ten anterior eye conditions, including anterior uveitis and herpes simplex keratitis. In England, community minor and urgent eye care is commissioned area by area. An evaluation published in July in [Ophthalmic and Physiological Optics](https://doi.org/10.1007/s44402-026-00137-w) found that fewer than 1 in 100 urgent eyecare cases in Greater Manchester in 2024 were managed as prescribing cases.

In the same evaluation, eye emergency optometrists at Manchester Royal Eye Hospital went back through 120 urgent referrals, knowing the hospital's diagnosis. They judged that a prescribing optometrist might have managed 40% of them in practice. What a red eye can be given on the NHS depends on which side of the border it is on.
What an independent prescribing optometrist can do in Scotland

Any optometrist in Scotland can examine and treat a red or sore eye under the NHS. In [Public Health Scotland's figures](https://www.publichealthscotland.scot/publications/ophthalmic-workload-statistics/general-ophthalmic-services-gos-activity-statistics-statistics-as-at-year-ending-march-2026/), anterior eye conditions were 30.0% of supplementary examinations in 2025/26. The General Ophthalmic Services (GOS) Specialist Supplementary service, which started on 1 August 2025, adds a second stage of treatment. Only a specialist independent prescribing (IP) optometrist or specialist ophthalmic medical practitioner, approved by their health board, can claim for it. Examples are a topical steroid and cycloplegic for anterior uveitis, or a sterile needle to remove a corneal foreign body and its rust ring. [The first appointment pays £97.69](https://www.publications.scot.nhs.uk/files/pca2026-o-01.pdf), and each follow-up pays £47.80.

In 2025/26, Public Health Scotland counted 10,267 first-appointment claims and 10,880 follow-up claims. Access depends on an approved prescriber nearby: when [the Scottish Government's impact assessment](https://www.gov.scot/publications/nhs-gos-scotland-amendment-regulations-2025-bria/) was written, no IP optometrist or ophthalmic medical practitioner provided GOS in Orkney, so the service could not run there. The assessment expects up to 20,000 unscheduled hospital appointments a year to move into the community once the service is fully rolled out. From summer 2029, optometrists graduating in Scotland, and nowhere else in the UK, will be able to qualify as independent prescribers.
What England commissions, and where

England's community minor and urgent eye care runs as the Community Urgent Eyecare Service (CUES) or the Minor Eye Conditions Service (MECS), depending on the area. [The College of Optometrists said in May 2025](https://www.college-optometrists.org/news/2025/may/lack-of-funding-threatens-urgent-care-in-england) that these services, with or without prescribing, were available in 73% of England. In Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, it said, every patient had access.

Greater Manchester commissions the service in all ten of its localities. In 2024 it saw 54,994 cases, and 83.4% stayed in primary care. Only 496 cases, 0.9%, were prescribing cases, in which the practitioner used their prescribing qualification. An IP optometrist managed 460 of them, and an ophthalmologist the other 36. Prescribing was offered at 23 practices, 10.4% of those in the service. Of the prescribing cases an IP optometrist managed, 87.5% ended in discharge, against 78.1% of other cases. The prescribing cases had been triaged as suitable for a prescriber, so the two groups are not alike.
What registrants told the GOC

The General Optical Council's [2026 registrant survey](https://optical.org/resource/registrant-workforce-and-perceptions-survey-2026.html) counts dispensing opticians and students as well as optometrists, and had 310 replies from Scotland. Its figures for working registrants rest on 276 in Scotland and 2,252 in England. Those in Scotland were less likely to have felt under pressure to meet commercial targets at the expense of patient care (25% against 32%), or to be considering leaving the profession over the next 12 to 24 months (8% against 16%). They were more likely to have felt unable to cope with their workload in the last 12 months (66% against 58%).
Why it matters in practice

In England, the first step before a red eye goes to eye casualty is knowing whether the local CUES or MECS has a prescribing pathway, and which practice nearby runs it. The College says registered optometrists are already qualified for minor and urgent eye care. It wants the service commissioned everywhere, extra entry requirements dropped or minimised, and optometrists able to give treatments without involving the GP. [Denmark's OCT pathway](/news/denmark-oct-teleophthalmology-referrals) raised the same question for scans.

In Scotland, a practice without a prescriber still manages the first stage, and refers the patient for the second to a practice listed on NHS Inform. Whether the service is moving patients out of hospital is not yet visible. Scottish optometrists referred over 119,500 patients to hospital in 2025/26. Public Health Scotland calls this a stable trend, in line with the rise in eye examinations.
The caveats

items: Greater Manchester is one region in one year, from routine records, and its discharge rates are not adjusted for case mix.
The 40% rests on 120 referrals to one hospital, rated afterwards with the hospital's diagnosis known. Missed diagnoses among discharged patients, and cost, were not measured.
Public Health Scotland counts claims paid since 1 August 2025, not patients treated, and no outcomes are published yet.
The GOC survey is self-reported, with an 11% response rate. Scotland's 8% is 23 of 276 working registrants, and nothing in the survey ties a gap to scope of practice.

seo.metaDescription: In a review of AI in eye care, 27 of 29 results top 90%. What is really stopping it in UK practice, and who carries the risk.
seo.metaTitle: AI in eye care: who is liable when it is wrong

keyPoints: A systematic review of AI reading fundus photographs lists 27 of 29 results above 90% in its table, and finds three barriers: workflow and cost, black-box outputs, models that do not generalise.
It does not answer the liability question. A UK commission said eight days earlier that negligence claims are disproportionately likely to be brought against clinicians and providers.
In the GOC's 2026 survey, 76% of optometrists were concerned about their legal responsibility if AI gets it wrong, as many as about AI errors, and 65% rated their AI knowledge poor.
The change a practice can make this week is a record: what the AI provided, how it informed the decision, and when and why you preferred your own reasoning.

faq.a: A fundus camera photographs the back of the eye: the retina, optic disc and macula. Those images are what diabetic eye screening grades, and they are what the AI systems in this review were reading. The review excluded studies using OCT or the slit lamp, though at least two systems in its own performance table use OCT as well as fundus images.
faq.q: What is a fundus camera?

faq.a: Software that reads retinal photographs and flags the ones that look abnormal, either as a first grader or as a triage step before a person looks. In research it performs well: 27 of the 29 results in this review's performance table are above 90%. In UK practice it is still rare: in the General Optical Council's 2026 survey, 8% of working registrants said they used AI of any kind to support a diagnosis, and 60% used it for none of the tasks listed.
faq.q: What is AI fundus screening?

faq.a: Not in the English programme. A 2020 independent evaluation of the EyeArt algorithm read 30,405 consecutive episodes across three English programmes and found referable retinopathy with 95.7% sensitivity, classifying all 462 cases of moderate-to-severe or proliferative disease as test-positive, including images it could not read. It agreed with the human grade of non-referable in only 54.0%, and its authors were testing it alongside human grading, not in place of it. Scotland's programme then used a computer to triage macular images. The UK National Screening Committee still did not recommend automated grading on 1 October 2026; its consultation closed on 3 August.
faq.q: Does the NHS use AI for diabetic eye screening?

faq.a: That depends on the facts, and it is not settled. What the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare found in September 2026 is that negligence claims are disproportionately likely to be brought against healthcare professionals and providers, because they hold the clearest duty of care, which it calls a perceived liability sink. Its Recommendation 28 asks that the contract between manufacturer and provider set out who delivers which risk controls. The College of Optometrists is plain about the clinical side: responsibility for the decision stays with the clinician, who must keep oversight and be able to overrule the software.
faq.q: Who is liable if an AI tool gets a diagnosis wrong?

body.text: AI in eye care does well in research. [A systematic review published on 18 September in the International Journal of Ophthalmology](https://doi.org/10.18240/ijo.2026.09.17) read 34 studies of AI reading fundus photographs. In its own performance table, 27 of the 29 results are above 90%, though the column it labels accuracy also holds sensitivities and an area under the curve.

What it does not answer is who carries the risk. It names medicolegal liability as a concern, but its results give three barriers and no analysis of who is liable. Eight days earlier, an independent commission set up by the MHRA reported on exactly that, and the GOC says it will respond.
What the review did

A PRISMA review, not a meta-analysis. Scopus, PubMed and Web of Science were searched to June 2025, and 34 studies were included, three of them from the UK. Diabetic retinopathy was the commonest subject, in 25 of them. Studies using OCT or the slit lamp were excluded. On the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool, 22 studies were moderate to high quality and 12 showed notable limitations.
What it found, and what it left out

Three barriers. The software does not fit the working day: separate programs, manual uploads, hardware that costs money. Clinicians cannot see how a black box reached its answer, which the authors tie to low trust. And models trained on one population do not travel, so performance falls in the groups already least well served. Their summary is blunt.
AI performs well in research (>90% accuracy) but falters in real-world use.

One hospital's simulation put numbers on the trade. [A study published in PLOS Digital Health on 15 September](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pdig.0001700) let AI clear its own negatives on 6,904 fundus photographs read by three retina specialists. The images needing a specialist fell to 7.3%–8.0% for diabetic retinopathy, and mean sensitivity for it fell from 0.9168 to 0.8838. In an exploratory analysis across all three diseases, 27.7%–30.1% still needed one. A stricter threshold won back most of the diabetic retinopathy loss, so where to set it is a clinical judgement as much as a technical one.
Who is liable when AI in eye care is wrong

[The National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-commission-into-the-regulation-of-ai-in-healthcare-recommendations-for-a-future-regulatory-framework/national-commission-into-the-regulation-of-ai-in-healthcare-recommendations-for-a-future-regulatory-framework) reported on 10 September with 44 recommendations. Under negligence as it stands, it found, claims are disproportionately likely to be brought against healthcare professionals and providers, because they have the clearest duty of care. It calls the result a perceived “liability sink”. Recommendation 28 is that the contract between manufacturer and provider should set out who delivers which risk controls. That is a recommendation, not a requirement.

Optometrists have worked this out. In [the General Optical Council's 2026 registrant survey](https://optical.org/asset/7A4BF5B9%2D81F5%2D4657%2DBEC485376F5C1ED3/), 76% of the 2,064 optometrists who answered were concerned about their legal responsibility if something goes wrong, as many as were concerned about the AI making errors, and 65% rated their own knowledge of AI as poor.
Why it matters in practice

What changes is not the consulting room but what you ask a supplier and what you write down. [The College of Optometrists' interim position](https://www.college-optometrists.org/policy-and-influencing/position-statements/interim-position-on-the-use-of-ai) says, among other things, three you can act on. Check the tool is registered with the MHRA as Artificial Intelligence as a Medical Device before you buy it. Tell patients when AI is being used, and where possible let them opt out. And keep records of what the AI provided, how it informed the decision, and when and why you preferred your own reasoning. That last one you can do this week.

The contract is the next renewal's job. The third is what to tell the patient who asks whether a computer will read their photographs. In NHS diabetic eye screening in England it will not yet, though the UK National Screening Committee is closer than it was: the evidence summary it consulted on concludes that some systems are as good as a first human grader and could be tested in real NHS services. That consultation closed on 3 August 2026, and no updated recommendation had been published by 1 October. For anything else, the answer is whatever your own practice's software does. What reaches the high street, to my mind, arrives inside a pathway, as [Denmark's OCT roll-out](/news/denmark-oct-teleophthalmology-referrals) did, not as a box on its own.
The caveats

items: The review's arithmetic does not hold together: the abstract says 34 studies from 2018 to 2025, the results say 2016 to 2025, and the table lists 29 entries, nine of them dated 2026. One of those reads fundus and OCT together, which its own exclusion criteria rule out. It states no limitations of its own.

The table's figures are each entry's own, mostly on curated data, never pooled, and not all are accuracies: some are sensitivities, one an area under the curve. Two rows cite reviews; the lowest, 73.0%, cites a news report. One model fell from 98.84% to 87.13% on outside data. None measures sight saved.
The Commission is an independent expert advisory body set up by the MHRA. Its 44 recommendations are not law, the government response is still to come, and the liability passage is analysis, not law.

The GOC figures are self-reported by the 3,451 who answered, an 11% response rate. The triage simulation is single-centre, retrospective and Korean, part-funded by the software's maker, two of whose employees are authors.
